commenti.body:
I don't remember where I read this, but I think the key to understanding Barry Lyndon is to notice that the narrator is unreliable. Despite his authoritative voice, everything he describes is contradicted by the actions on the screen. Barry isn't a charlatan despite everyone perceiving him as one. He is very honorable and ambitious.

The narrator mentions his infidelities on Lady Lyndon, but doesn't mention the reconciliation between them because that was a private, unwitnessed moment. A lot of Barry's positive qualities are likewise ignored by the narrator.

From Lord Bullingdon's point of view, he returns home to save his mother from the dangerous social climber who swindled her. But in reality, he is just a jealous boy who separated his mother from a good man who loved her. The duel just demonstrates the difference between the cowardly Bullingdon and the honorable Barry.

I felt there were two ways to view Barry's final duel. One is the viewpoint you espouse. The other view is that Barry had simply lost the will to do anything at all, and sought death in whatever form he could. So he threw away his shot and waited for Bullington to hit him.

I tend to lean towards the first one, however. It feels more narratively satisfying.

Lol, if you think Barry is a good person you've misread the movie entirely. He's not evil, but he's the ultimate opportunist: he sees a chance to gain money, to escape his situation, to gain some pleasure, and he takes that chance every single time, honor and consequences be dammed. Sometimes that opportunism works out, sometimes it doesn't.

He is opportunistic, but I don't see how that makes him a bad person. He was a very idealistic young man, and the world punished him for that. He had to adapt to the world around him in order to survive. Still, the film goes out of its way to show us qualities that are incongruent with him being a simple upstart.

First of all, the incident that starts him on his journey showcases his bravery and naivety. He doesn't desert the army out of cowardice. He does it because his friend and father figure is killed. His affair with the peasant woman was genuine, not just an opportunistic chance to get pleasure. They were both lonely people looking for comfort.

The narrator doesn't explain how Barry gained the trust of the Chevalier. Then, the film shows how it happened. Barry gains his trust by a sincere outpouring of emotion. Likewise, his relationship with Lady Lyndon was more honest than is implied by the voice over.

A lot of the decisions he takes that seem calculated are then shown to be emotional. His last act of kindness, sparing Lord Bullingdon's life, is punished by disability, seclusion and infamy.

I appreciate your thoughts, but I disagree.

A lot of what I’ve seen written online about *Barry Lyndon* I think kind of misses the point. I do not think Redmond is a villain or an anti-hero. I don’t think that’s how WMT wrote him, I don’t think that’s how Kubrick portrayed him.

I think Redmond acts “honorably” at plenty of points throughout the story, or at least you can make the argument. He fought for what he thought was love, forcing him to leave his home. He exhibited bravery through desertion, which is a wonderful bit of irony. He showed loyalty to his countrymen when he sided with the Chevalier du Balibari at great personal risk. By the time Redmond is making his bones cheating at gambling, his nihilism is very understandable given what he has experienced: he (accurately) views the world as dog-eat-dog and wants to chase his pleasures.

I don’t think the fact that he’s a philandering husband, irresponsible financier, and a bit of a bully to his stepson wipes out all of his positive traits. Nor do I think Lord Bullingdon is purely in the wrong; as obnoxious as he is, he’s standing up for his mother (although he kind of does it just for his own benefit imo).

I strongly disagree that this film is a takedown of the ruling class or an indictment of economic inequality or that somehow Redmond is meant to be thought of as purely a scoundrel and a monster. I think there is some satire and mockery built in, but I think this film at its heart is about the rise and fall of a regular-ass person. Icarus had a fatal flaw, but he was also a dreamer and is, in some ways, admirable.

But I do absolutely love that final duel and its cruel irony.

I completely agree. I think the film establishes that the world bullies him into his nihilism. By the time he meets Lady Lyndon, he is completely disillusioned about love, honor, bravery, the law…he’s just behaving like everyone else.

The duel is a lose-lose. He either murders his stepson in an illegal duel or is killed.

I believe his act of kindness was an attempt at reconciliation or as the characters ask, “if the gentleman is satisfied.”

It’s ultimately the stepson who refuses to drop the issue and in his incompetence wounds him instead of doing him the service of releasing him from his grief.

Both ideas feed into each other. The life that Barry led made him realize it wasn't worth living this way in the end. In that moment, he was ready to give up on this life and by doing so, he lived in the way he believed he ought to when he was young, the challenge gave him an opportunity to change. He reconnected with his ideals. It resonates with what Kubrick said in an interview, that since god doesn't exist and a man ultimately loses faith in the goodness of mankind, only by being strong enough can we build our own light in the middle of that dark night. Something like that. Barry Lindon is the journey of such a realization, though it's not all that happy in the end.

He's not a Tony Soprano type antihero with no redeeming qualities, but he's a very selfish person for the most part.

The first duel and his childish behavior stemming from jealousy, the way he blows smoke in his wife's face, his favoritism towards his biological son, etc etc. And it's not just an innocuous type of opportunism. Selfishness or general disregard for others are always a part of it.

But he is often surrounded by other flawed characters too. I think the point it's making is more about how high society isn't actually as civilized as we like to think rather than saying Redmond Barry in particular is a bad person

In a lot of the situations you mention, he was either in the right or he made amends for his mistakes. His childish behavior in the first duel is understandable given that he was a child.

I think his treatment of Lady Lyndon early in their marriage, while unjustifiable, was due to his sense of inferiority. Her entire inner circle rejected him and didn't try to hide it. Him lashing out at her is obviously unfair. However, they do reconcile before the time jump. They remain on good terms until they lose their youngest child.

As for his favoritism, the conflict between Barry and Bullingdon preceded the birth of Barry's biological son. I think Lord Bullingdon bears more responsibility for their animosity than Barry. There was no world where Bullingdon would accept Barry as his stepfather, and Barry knew it. He is openly disrespectful and antagonistic towards him for no reason. The final straw in their relationship where Barry punishes Bullingdon for his son's mistake is more due to their history than favoritism, in my opinion.

I think it shows that luck is all there is to being rich or poor. 

When Barry does the right thing he loses his leg and his kingdom. Mist if the movie is right place right time. 

But in the end who cares what you have and how he got there, we are all equal in death.
Yeah, Barry is kind of a dick, but Lord Bullingdon is just the fucking worst.

I think there's an interesting third. He has learned from his first duel that killing someone in a duel can turn people against you. Remembering that lesson , he calculated that killing his step son would make him a social pariah. More than he already was. The hail Mary pass here is to let his step son live and maybe he regains social standing again.

I've always understood that deliberately shooting toward the ground was not so much an act of kindness, but very much an insult toward the other party. It's basically telling the other person "You're not worth it." Which is very much in line with how Barry treated Bullington his entire life.

I mean, I guess the genius of it all is that it's an action that's really hard to decipher what the true meaning of it is. So much of the movie is saying things without actually saying things.

I feel like it's not totally fair to say Bullingdon is acting out of base level vengeance.  It's pretty clear that, in his mind, he's facing death in an attempt to save his family.  


Barry is burning through the estate's finances, his foolishness got Bullingdon's brother killed (though it's unclear if he had any fondness for the kid), and driven Bullingdon's mother to attempt suicide.  You could say Bullingdon is just trying to save his own inheritance and reputation, but he's clearly willing to risk death over it despite being outclassed and terrified.
That's the one. I didn't want to pass it off as my original observation because that essay made me reconsider my reading of the film.

The film is filled with games of chance, people playing cards, and scenes which stress the role of luck, fate and determinism.

Throughout the film, zoom-outs are also repeatedly used to put Barry in context; he shrinks, while the larger material world acting upon him takes emphasis.

So for three hours, you watch this guy at the mercy of the cosmos, and propelled by fate and blind chance. It's Kubrick's "The Killing" writ large. But then, Barry makes the ironic choice to exercise free will, by relinquishing it. By submitting to the dice roll. To the laws of the cosmos. It's one of his few virtuous and righteous acts, but of course he's punished for this. The universe is cruel. 

These themes are then giving a large context. Barry's a social climber who seeks to be better than others (in terms of money, status and so on). The climax of the duel ironically critiques this illusion of rugged individualism, and rubber stamps it with the final images we see: the date, and its "they're all equal now", points to the oncoming French revolution, and the attacks on the egotistical presumptions of Barry's entire social class.
